## Research question

Do country population characteristics and continent help explain differences
in per-capita CO2 emissions? This analysis uses multiple linear regression to
study the association between 2019 CO2 emissions per person and population
size, population density, annual population growth, and continent.

The analysis is observational: its results describe associations and do not
show that population characteristics cause emissions to change.

## Data and preparation

The analysis combines the repository's `CO2_emission.csv` and
`world_population.csv` files using their three-letter country codes. The
emissions file contains CO2 emissions in metric tons per person and has two
columns labeled 2019; the first is used. Population size, density, growth
rate, and continent come from the population file. Rows missing any analysis
variable, and rows with non-positive values for a logged variable, are
excluded.

```{r prepare-data}
population <- read.csv("datasets/world_population.csv", check.names = FALSE)
emissions_raw <- read.csv("datasets/CO2_emission.csv", check.names = FALSE)

year_2019 <- which(names(emissions_raw) == "2019")
if (length(year_2019) == 0) {
  stop("The emissions dataset does not contain a 2019 column.")
}
if (length(year_2019) > 1 &&
    !isTRUE(all.equal(
      emissions_raw[[year_2019[1]]],
      emissions_raw[[year_2019[2]]],
      check.attributes = FALSE
    ))) {
  stop("The duplicate 2019 emissions columns do not match.")
}

if (anyDuplicated(population$CCA3) || anyDuplicated(emissions_raw$country_code)) {
  stop("Country codes must be unique within each dataset.")
}

population_for_join <- data.frame(
  code = population$CCA3,
  population_2022 = population[["2022 Population"]],
  density = population[["Density (per km²)"]],
  growth_factor = population[["Growth Rate"]],
  continent = population$Continent
)
emissions_for_join <- data.frame(
  code = emissions_raw$country_code,
  co2_per_capita_2019 = emissions_raw[[year_2019[1]]]
)

joined <- merge(population_for_join, emissions_for_join, by = "code")
analysis_data <- joined[
  complete.cases(joined) &
    joined$population_2022 > 0 &
    joined$density > 0 &
    joined$co2_per_capita_2019 > 0,
]
analysis_data$continent <- relevel(
  factor(analysis_data$continent),
  ref = "Africa"
)
analysis_data$log_co2 <- log(analysis_data$co2_per_capita_2019)
analysis_data$log_population <- log(analysis_data$population_2022)
analysis_data$log_density <- log(analysis_data$density)
analysis_data$growth_percent <- (analysis_data$growth_factor - 1) * 100

if (nrow(analysis_data) == 0) {
  stop("No complete, positive observations are available for the model.")
}

model <- lm(
  log_co2 ~ log_population + log_density + growth_percent + continent,
  data = analysis_data
)
model_summary <- summary(model)
```

The model contains `r nrow(analysis_data)` countries. Its response is the
natural logarithm of 2019 per-capita emissions. Natural logarithms are used
for emissions, population size, and density because these measures span wide
ranges and emissions are right-skewed. The growth-rate variable is expressed
as an annual percentage (for example, a growth factor of 1.02 is 2%).

## Model

The fitted model is:

\[
\log(\text{CO2 per capita}) =
\beta_0 + \beta_1\log(\text{population}) +
\beta_2\log(\text{density}) + \beta_3(\text{growth percent}) +
\text{continent effects} + \epsilon.
\]

Africa is the reference continent. Each coefficient estimates the association
with emissions while holding the other variables in the model constant.

```{r model-results}
coefficient_table <- as.data.frame(coef(model_summary))
coefficient_table$term <- rownames(coefficient_table)
confidence_intervals <- confint(model)
coefficient_table$lower_95 <- confidence_intervals[
  coefficient_table$term, 1
]
coefficient_table$upper_95 <- confidence_intervals[
  coefficient_table$term, 2
]
rownames(coefficient_table) <- NULL
names(coefficient_table) <- c(
  "Estimate", "Std. error", "t value", "p value", "Term",
  "95% CI lower", "95% CI upper"
)
coefficient_table <- coefficient_table[
  , c("Term", "Estimate", "Std. error", "95% CI lower", "95% CI upper", "p value")
]

knitr::kable(
  coefficient_table,
  digits = 3,
  caption = "Multiple regression coefficients and 95% confidence intervals"
)
```

The model explains `r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * model_summary$r.squared)`% of
the variation in log emissions (adjusted \(R^2\) =
`r sprintf("%.3f", model_summary$adj.r.squared)`). The predictors are
statistically associated with the response overall
(\(F\) = `r sprintf("%.2f", model_summary$fstatistic[1])`,
\(p\) = `r format.pval(
pf(model_summary$fstatistic[1], model_summary$fstatistic[2],
   model_summary$fstatistic[3], lower.tail = FALSE),
digits = 3
)`).

### Interpreting the coefficients

Because both emissions and population size are logged, the population
coefficient is an elasticity: a 1% increase in population is associated with
approximately a `r sprintf("%.2f", coef(model)["log_population"])`% change in
per-capita emissions, conditional on the other predictors. This association
is not statistically significant at the 5% level (\(p\) =
`r sprintf("%.3f", coef(model_summary)["log_population", "Pr(>|t|)"])`), so
these data do not provide clear evidence of an independent population-size
association after adjustment.

Likewise, a 1% increase in population density is associated with an
approximate `r sprintf("%.2f", coef(model)["log_density"])`% change in
per-capita emissions, holding the remaining variables constant. The
estimated association is negative and statistically significant at the 5%
level (\(p\) =
`r sprintf("%.3f", coef(model_summary)["log_density", "Pr(>|t|)"])`).

For annual growth, a one-percentage-point increase is associated with an
estimated `r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * (exp(coef(model)["growth_percent"]) - 1))`%
change in per-capita emissions, with other predictors held constant. The
estimated association is negative (\(p\) =
`r format.pval(
coef(model_summary)["growth_percent", "Pr(>|t|)"],
digits = 3
)`). This describes a conditional association in this sample, not a causal
effect.

The continent coefficients compare each continent with Africa after
adjustment for the numeric predictors. For example, the model's estimated
emissions ratio for Asia versus Africa is
`r sprintf("%.2f", exp(coef(model)["continentAsia"]))` to 1. The coefficient
table gives the corresponding estimates and confidence intervals for all
continents; these contrasts should not be interpreted as causal effects or as
within-continent comparisons.

## Model checks

Residual-versus-fitted and normal Q-Q plots are used to look for conspicuous
non-linearity, changing residual spread, or departures from normally
distributed errors. These plots are diagnostic aids rather than proof that
all model assumptions hold.

```{r diagnostics, fig.width=7, fig.height=3.5}
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(
  fitted(model), resid(model),
  xlab = "Fitted log emissions",
  ylab = "Residuals",
  main = "Residuals vs fitted"
)
abline(h = 0, lty = 2, col = "red")
qqnorm(resid(model), main = "Normal Q-Q plot")
qqline(resid(model), col = "red")
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

## Conclusion and limitations

In this sample, density, annual population growth, and adjusted continent
contrasts show evidence of association with 2019 per-capita CO2 emissions;
the model does not find a statistically significant independent association
for population size at the 5% level. The \(R^2\) indicates that other
country-level factors remain important.

The data are cross-sectional, countries may differ in omitted factors such as
energy sources, industrial structure, and income, and the population
characteristics are from 2022 while emissions are from 2019. The analysis
therefore supports association statements only, and the time mismatch and
unmeasured confounding limit interpretation. Results also apply only to
countries with complete data in both files.
